chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, and Muhammad ibn Ismail, from Al-Fadl ibn Shazan, all together from Ibn Abi Umeyr, from Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Hajjaj, from Aban ibn Taghlib, who said:

I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): 'What do you say regarding a man who cuts off a finger from the fingers of a woman? How much is its compensation?' He said: 'Ten camels.' I said: 'If he cuts off two?' He said: 'Twenty.' I said: 'If he cuts off three?' He said: 'Thirty.' I said: 'If he cuts off four?' He said: 'Twenty.'

I said: 'Glory be to Allah! He cuts off three, so thirty is upon him, and he cuts off four, so twenty is upon him. This used to reach us while we were in Iraq, so we distanced ourselves from the one who said it, and we said that the one who brought it was a devil.'

So he said: 'Wait, O Aban! This is how the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) judged: The woman is equal to the man up to a third of the blood money. When it reaches the third, she returns to half. O Aban! You seized me with analogy (qiyas), but the Sunnah, when it is analogized, destroys the Religion.'

key_terms.الدِّيَة: Blood money or compensation for injury/death

ai.seo_question: What is the difference between blood money for a woman's fingers and a man's, and how does analogy affect it?
ai.summary: This hadith from Al-Kafi illustrates the principle of 'Tafaddul' (disproportionate increase) in female blood money, where the compensation for three fingers (30 camels) exceeds that for four (20 camels), a ruling derived from the specific proportion of a woman's total diyah being two-thirds of a man's. Imam al-Sadiq (AS) uses this to critique Aban’s reliance on linear analogy (qiyas), emphasizing that in Shia jurisprudence, the revealed Sunnah’s specific metrics take precedence over rational deduction when they diverge. This highlights the distinct epistemological stance of the Ahl al-Bayt, where divine legislation can supersede human logical consistency.
